title: Recognise basic breeding behaviour of farm animals

lessons.title: What is heat?
lessons.html:
Heat means ready to mate

A female animal can only fall pregnant at certain times. This time is called heat (or oestrus). When she is on heat she will let the male mount her. If she is not on heat, she will walk away or fight him.

Heat comes back again and again until the female is pregnant. This is called the heat cycle. In cows, sheep, goats and pigs the cycle comes back about every three weeks. Heat itself lasts only a short time, often less than a day, so you must watch carefully.

Why it matters

  • If a heat is missed, the farmer loses about three weeks.
  • A cow that does not calve every year costs the farmer money.
  • When artificial insemination is used, the person doing it must know which cows are on heat.

When to watch

Watch the animals at least two times a day, early in the morning and late in the afternoon. Animals show heat signs more when it is cool and quiet. Watch for about twenty to thirty minutes each time.

Each animal must have a number or tag so that you can tell your supervisor exactly which one is on heat.

lessons.title: Signs of heat in different animals
lessons.html:
Cows

  • Stands still when another cow mounts her. This is the best sign.
  • Tries to mount other cows.
  • Restless, walks a lot, bellows (calls).
  • Clear, stringy slime from the vulva.
  • Swollen, red vulva.
  • Hair rubbed off on the tail head from being mounted.
  • Eats less, may give less milk.

Ewes and does (sheep and goats)

  • Signs are hard to see. Ewes stay near the ram.
  • Does wag their tails a lot and bleat.
  • Farmers often use a ram with a crayon harness. The crayon marks the ewe's rump when he mounts her.

Sows (pigs)

  • Red, swollen vulva.
  • Restless, grunts, may not eat.
  • When you press firmly on her back she stands very still. This is called the standing reflex.
  • Standing still near the boar.

Mares (horses)

  • Lifts tail, passes small amounts of urine.
  • Shows interest in the stallion.

What to do

  1. Note the animal's number and the time you saw the sign.
  2. Tell your supervisor quickly.
  3. Write it in the heat book.

Do not chase or shout at animals to see if they are on heat. Stress hides heat signs. Move quietly among them and let them behave normally. On some farms tail paint or heat patches are put on cows. When a cow is mounted the paint rubs off or the patch changes colour. Check these every time you walk past and tell your supervisor which cows have rubbed paint.

lessons.title: Males, mating and safety
lessons.html:
Male behaviour

Bulls, rams, bucks, boars and stallions smell and follow females that are on heat. A male may lift his top lip and smell the air. This is called flehmen. He will follow the female and then mount her.

Signs a female is pregnant

  • She does not come back on heat after about three weeks.
  • Later her belly gets bigger and her udder grows.
  • The vet can test to make sure. This is called pregnancy testing.

Safety with breeding animals

Breeding males are strong and can be dangerous, especially when females are on heat.

  • Never turn your back on a bull, ram or boar.
  • Never go alone into a camp or pen with a bull. Always know where the escape route is.
  • Be careful of cows that are mounting each other. They can knock you down.
  • Sows with piglets and cows with new calves protect their young. Keep a safe distance.
  • Wash your hands after touching the back of an animal.

Report these problems

  • A female that never comes on heat.
  • A female that comes on heat again and again.
  • A male that does not want to mate, or is lame.
  • Pus or blood from the vulva or sheath.

Key points

  • Heat is the short time a female is ready to mate.
  • Cows, sheep, goats and pigs come on heat about every three weeks.
  • A cow that stands still when mounted is on heat.
  • Watch at least twice a day and write down the number and time.
  • Never turn your back on a breeding male.
